what_it_does: Modern computers waste enormous energy shuttling data back and forth between the processor and memory — a problem called the 'memory wall.' ARCANE proposes a new way to reduce this waste by placing small, specialized math units physically inside or very close to the memory itself, a technique called compute-near-memory (doing arithmetic right where the data lives rather than dragging it across a slow, power-hungry bus). These near-memory units are wired into the processor's own cache system (the fast on-chip scratchpad that holds recently used data), so ordinary programs can issue custom instructions that silently trigger the near-memory math without the programmer needing to shuffle data by hand. The design uses the open-source RISC-V processor standard and targets flexible, general-purpose workloads — not just one fixed application. Based on the abstract alone it is not yet clear how large the real-world energy or speed gains are.
